caption: Wind and thick cloud at sunset over the Chajnantor plateau, ALMA Observatory, Chile
story: Heavy cloud rolls in over the high plateau of Chajnantor as the Sun goes down, pushed along by strong winds and lit in fiery colours. The plateau sits 5000 metres above sea level in the Chilean Andes and hosts the 66 antennas of the ALMA Observatory, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array.

Cloud is a rare visitor over these skies. ESO Photo Ambassador Babak Tafreshi took the picture while on the ESO 2016 Fulldome Expedition, a trip that gathered images for the ESO Supernova Planetarium & Visitor Centre.

The clouds ALMA is built to study are of a very different kind. Molecular clouds are huge gatherings of gas and dust, so cold that they sit just a few tens of degrees above absolute zero. Many of these star-forming regions look dark and hidden in visible light, yet they glow brightly at millimetre and submillimetre wavelengths, the light ALMA collects.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph of the ALMA site by Babak Tafreshi. The source gives no camera or colour details.
understand.eye: The antennas themselves work at millimetre and submillimetre wavelengths, which the eye cannot see, while this photograph records ordinary visible light.

alt: Thick cloud lit in fiery colours at sunset over the high Chajnantor plateau, home of the ALMA antennas.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 105, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The spiral galaxy NGC 105 seems to be ploughing edge-on into a long, thin neighbour. The collision is an illusion. The two only line up by chance on the sky, and the elongated galaxy lies much farther off and has drawn little attention from astronomers. NGC 105 itself is roughly 215 million light-years away in Pisces.
Chance alignments like this are common. The stars of a constellation sit at very different distances from Earth and only look like a group from our viewpoint.

Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 took these data as part of a large set of observations of nearby galaxies that hold both Cepheid variables and supernovae. One is a class of pulsating star and the other the explosive death of a massive star, but both have predictable luminosities. Comparing their real brightness with how bright they look gives a distance. Because NGC 105 contains both, astronomers can check the two methods against each other.
explore: Distances to galaxies including NGC 105 went into measuring the rate at which the Universe expands, known as the Hubble constant. The result disagrees with the most widely accepted cosmological model, and the analysis puts the odds that measurement errors caused the mismatch at only 1 in a million. The source says this adds persuasive evidence that the standard model of cosmology is wrong or incomplete.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed NGC 105 in visible and near-infrared light, through filters from 350 nm to 1.6 μm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared light, which the eye cannot see, and Hubble's long exposures reveal far fainter detail than any eye could.

alt: A spiral galaxy seen nearly edge-on beside a thinner, elongated galaxy that appears to touch it.

caption: The Milky Way, the Magellanic Clouds and airglow over the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory
story: The Milky Way arches over one of the Auxiliary Telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope, with the two Magellanic Clouds beside it. Along the horizon runs a faint green and red shimmer of airglow, light the atmosphere gives off by itself and that shows only under very dark skies. To the left, the zodiacal light rises like a white brushstroke.

French astrophotographer Julien Looten made this 360-degree panorama during a visit to the VLT at Cerro Paranal in Chile, a place with one of the darkest skies on Earth. One of the VLT's Unit Telescopes adds laser beams to the scene. They help correct the blurring caused by turbulence in the atmosphere.

Looten comes from northern France, where cloud and light pollution often spoil the sky. He described being so overwhelmed by the view that he forgot everything around him, with the galactic bulge shining straight overhead. He called the night one of the most beautiful of his life.

understand.summary: This is a 360-degree panoramic landscape photograph by Julien Looten. The source gives no details of camera settings or colour processing.
understand.eye: Airglow shows only under very dark skies, and the source does not say how the photograph's colours compare with the naked-eye view.

alt: A 360-degree night-sky panorama with the Milky Way arching over an Auxiliary Telescope, the two Magellanic Clouds beside it, laser beams from a Unit Telescope, and a faint green and red glow along the horizon.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 4535, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Long spiral arms flecked with bluish colour wind around a yellower central bulge in NGC 4535, a barred spiral about 50 million light-years from Earth in the constellation Virgo. Through a small telescope the galaxy looks faint and ghostly, which is why the amateur astronomer Leland S. Copeland nicknamed it the Lost Galaxy in the 1950s.

Hubble's sharp view shows how colour can reveal a galaxy's stars. The blue tones scattered through the arms point to many young, hot stars. The yellow glow of the bulge suggests the centre is home mostly to older, cooler stars.
Hubble observed the galaxy for the PHANGS survey, which aims to clarify how cold gas clouds and star formation relate to the shapes and other properties of galaxies.
explore: The PHANGS-HST Collection had its first public release on 11 January 2021. The Hubble observations of NGC 4535 used Wide Field Camera 3 with filters running from the ultraviolet through visible light.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed NGC 4535 through ultraviolet and visible-light filters from 275 nm to 814 nm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Ultraviolet light is invisible to the eye, and through a small telescope this galaxy looks hazy and ghostly rather than detailed and coloured.

alt: A barred spiral galaxy with long arms dotted with blue patches around a yellowish central bulge.

caption: The Butterfly Galaxies NGC 4567 and NGC 4568, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: Two galaxies, NGC4567 and NGC4568, have just begun to collide and merge. Their wing-like outline earned the pair the nickname the Butterfly Galaxies. The pair sits in Virgo, at a distance of around 60 million light-years.

Such collisions are common in the Universe. They sound violent, but the source describes them as surprisingly peaceful, with gravity guiding the stars, gas and dust as they rearrange. Scientists think the Milky Way will one day go through a similar encounter with our neighbour, the Andromeda Galaxy.

The image comes from FORS2, the FOcal Reducer and low dispersion Spectrograph 2, mounted on ESO's Very Large Telescope at Paranal Observatory in the Chilean Andes. FORS2 is so versatile that it is nicknamed Paranal's Swiss Army knife. As well as taking pictures, it can record spectra of up to several tens of objects at once or study polarised light.
explore: The picture was made for the ESO Cosmic Gems programme, which uses telescope time that cannot serve science observations to image interesting or visually appealing objects for education and outreach. The data may still be useful for research and are available to astronomers through ESO's science archive.

understand.summary: FORS2 on the Very Large Telescope observed the galaxies in visible light through b, v, R and hydrogen-alpha filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The hydrogen-alpha filter isolates the glow of hydrogen gas, and the telescope's exposures collect far more light than an eye could from such distant galaxies.

alt: Two colliding galaxies whose combined outline resembles a pair of wings.

caption: The galaxy cluster Abell 2218, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble picture shows Abell 2218, a massive cluster of galaxies that the source likens to a giant magnifying glass in space. Seen in the direction of Draco, the cluster is some 2 billion light-years from Earth.

The comparison refers to gravitational lensing. A cluster this heavy bends and brightens the light of galaxies that sit far behind it, so objects that would otherwise be too faint to study can be seen. That is why the cluster is catalogued as an example of gravitationally lensed galaxies in the early Universe.

The image has a place in Hubble's own history. It was among the first views the telescope took after the servicing mission of December 1999, when Hubble returned to scanning the sky. A galaxy cluster is a large gathering of galaxies bound by gravity, and the more mass it holds, the more strongly it bends light.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 observed Abell 2218 in visible and near-infrared light through filters at 450, 606 and 814 nm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The galaxies here are far too faint for the eye, and Hubble's exposures gather light from them that no eyepiece view could show.

alt: The massive galaxy cluster Abell 2218, with many galaxies across the frame.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 7541, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope captured NGC 7541, a barred spiral galaxy in the constellation Pisces. It lies about 110 million light-years away and forms a pair with its nearby companion, NGC 7537.

In a barred spiral, the spiral arms wrap around a bright centre crossed by a bar of gas and stars. The bar is thought to stir up the central region and feed processes such as star formation and active galactic nuclei, which might otherwise never begin or might have stalled. As many as two-thirds of spiral galaxies may have bars, the Milky Way among them.
NGC 7541 forms stars faster than usual. That supports the idea that bars act as stellar nurseries, gathering gas and funnelling it inwards where it can build new stars.

understand.summary: The image combines observations from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3 in visible and near-infrared light, from 350 nm to 1.6 μm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared light, which the eye cannot see, and Hubble's exposures gather far more light than an eye can.

alt: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 7541, with spiral arms around a central bar.

caption: The ram-pressure stripped tail of the galaxy D100, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope and the Subaru Telescope
story: A plume of gas trails away from the spiral galaxy nicknamed D100. The image shows only part of the tail, which extends well beyond the frame to the left. It combines data from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys with data from the Subaru Telescope in Hawaii.

D100 belongs to the huge Coma cluster, and its tail is the product of ram-pressure stripping. The space between a cluster's galaxies is far from empty. It holds very hot gas and plasma, known as the intracluster medium, that drags at galaxies as they travel through it, much like the resistance you feel wading through deep water. This pressure has pulled gas out of D100 and drawn it into a long plume.
The effect can be powerful enough to pull galaxies to pieces, leaving some with bizarre shapes. Crowded clusters such as Coma, home to thousands of galaxies, are ideal places to study it.
explore: Ram-pressure stripping matters beyond its looks. By removing gas, it can have a profound effect on how galaxies change and on whether they go on forming new generations of stars.

understand.summary: This combines visible-light Hubble data from the Advanced Camera for Surveys, at 475 nm and 814 nm, with data from the Subaru Telescope. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The combined Hubble and Subaru exposures collect far more light than an eye can.

alt: A spiral galaxy with a long plume of gas streaming away from it to one side.

caption: The ESO 3.6-metre telescope and a rock with prehistoric engravings under moonlight, La Silla Observatory
story: A red rock fills the foreground, carved with prehistoric engravings, while behind it stands the ESO 3.6-metre telescope at La Silla Observatory in Chile. The Moon dominates the sky and shines brightly enough to light the whole scene.

Several engraved rocks lie around La Silla, and this one belongs to the richest site in the area. A full photographic and topographic survey of the carvings was carried out in 1990. Most show people and animals, along with puzzling geometric figures.

The carvings are believed to be the work of the El Molle complex, northern Chile's first culture. Geologists think the first millennium of our era was much wetter than today, so parts of the Atacama Desert, now very dry, could support settled communities.

understand.summary: This is a moonlit landscape photograph by Babak Tafreshi. The source gives no camera or colour details.
understand.eye: The eye sees little colour in dim light, while a camera can record colour, such as the red of the rock, even in a moonlit scene.

alt: A red rock with carved figures in the foreground and a telescope dome behind it under a bright Moon.

caption: A sun pillar over an ALMA antenna on the Chajnantor plateau, Chile
story: Reds and blues fill the sky over the Chajnantor plateau in Chile's Atacama Desert, and a sun pillar rises from the Sun in line with a large antenna. Clouds are a rare sight in this dry region, and they help create the colourful display.

A sun pillar is an optical effect produced by ice crystals in the atmosphere. The antenna in the photograph belongs to the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, or ALMA, which ESO co-owns. The Chajnantor plateau is its home.

ALMA is among the world's most powerful observatories for radio astronomy. It has a collection of 66 antennae, each one much like the antenna pictured, and the array has been responsible for many groundbreaking discoveries over the years. It also contributed to making the first image of a black hole.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph by C. Duran of an ALMA antenna under a cloudy sky. The source gives no camera or colour details.
understand.eye: The colours and the sun pillar are ordinary visible light, but the antenna itself observes radio wavelengths that the eye cannot see.

alt: A large dish antenna under a red and blue sky, with a vertical pillar of light rising from the Sun in line with it.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 157, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: A sweep of stars through the middle of NGC 157 traces a giant letter S, a shape that reminds the source of Superman's emblem. This spiral galaxy lies about 75 million light-years away in the constellation Cetus, the Sea Monster.

The picture was taken with HAWK-I, the High-Acuity Wide-field K-band Imager, on ESO's Very Large Telescope at Paranal Observatory in Chile. HAWK-I detects infrared light, which passes through the gas and dust that usually block our view. That lets astronomers look into dense regions where stars are forming, which would otherwise stay hidden.

Star formation matters for our own story too. The processes now gathering material together and making stars in NGC 157 also worked in the Milky Way around 4.5 billion years ago, when they formed the Sun. Studying them in another galaxy is a way of learning where we came from.
explore: NGC 157 is faint, at about magnitude 11, yet dedicated amateur astronomers can still track it down with their own telescopes. When the image was released, HAWK-I was described as one of the newest and most powerful instruments on the VLT.

understand.summary: HAWK-I on the Very Large Telescope observed NGC 157 in near-infrared light through Y, H and K filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, so the colours here are a translation of light no one could see directly.

alt: A spiral galaxy whose central band of stars curves into an S shape.

caption: The face-on spiral galaxy NGC 1309, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope photographed NGC 1309, a spiral galaxy that faces us nearly head-on so its arms can be seen in full. The galaxy lies 100 million light-years, or 30 megaparsecs, from Earth.
NGC 1309 does not live alone. It is one of about 200 members of the Eridanus group of galaxies, a loose gathering of galaxies held together by their mutual gravity.

The galaxy also hosted a stellar explosion. Light from the supernova SN 2002fk reached Earth in September 2002. A supernova is the violent death of a star, and for a while it can shine as brightly as a whole galaxy of ordinary stars. The face-on angle gives Hubble an unobstructed look at the galaxy's disc, recorded here in colour.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed NGC 1309 in visible and near-infrared light through filters at 435, 555 and 814 nm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared light, which the eye cannot see, and Hubble's exposures gather far more light than an eye can.

alt: The spiral galaxy NGC 1309, seen face-on.

caption: A laser guide star and light-painted letters at the Allgäu Public Observatory, Germany
story: On a clear night in Bavaria, a laser beam shoots straight up from the Allgäu Public Observatory in Ottobeuren, Germany, while the letters ESO glow in front of the building. Staff drew them in light with their mobile phones during the long exposure. The Milky Way appears just left of the beam, and dotted aircraft tracks cross the sky above the horizon.

The occasion was the filming of an ESOcast episode about ESO's new compact laser guide star unit. A laser guide star is an artificial star made in the atmosphere. The beam makes sodium atoms in a layer 90 kilometres up glow, and adaptive optics use measurements of that point of light to undo the blurring caused by the air.

The laser is powerful, at 20 watts. To protect pilots and passengers, the Deutsche Flugsicherung, which manages German air traffic control, set up a no-fly zone around the observatory during the night-time observing hours.
explore: ESO's patented and licensed design launches the laser through a small telescope, all in one modular unit that mounts directly on a large telescope. The VLT was to receive four such units, and the concept is also key to units for the future European Extremely Large Telescope. When filmed, this unit was being tested before shipping to Paranal.

understand.summary: This is a long-exposure photograph by M. Kornmesser, long enough for people to draw letters in light with phones. The source gives no other camera or colour details.
understand.eye: The long exposure turns moving lights, such as the phones and the aircraft, into streaks and dots that the eye would never see as a single picture.

alt: A vertical laser beam rising from an observatory at night, with the letters ESO drawn in light in front of it and the Milky Way to the left.

caption: The Carina Nebula, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope
story: This wide colour view of the Carina Nebula, also catalogued as NGC 3372, picks out fine detail in its stars and dust. Towards the bottom left sits Eta Carinae, a binary star that the source ranks among the most impressive anywhere in the Universe, with the well-known Keyhole Nebula right beside it.

Above and to the right of Eta Carinae lies Trumpler 14, an open star cluster made of very bright, young stars. A second open cluster, Collinder 228, sits just below Eta Carinae. Open clusters are loose groups of stars that formed together from the same cloud of gas.

The picture covers an area of sky 0.55 degrees on each side. At the nebula's distance of 7500 light-years, that amounts to a region 72 light-years across in each direction. North is at the top and east is to the left.
explore: The image was made with the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope, and it is also sold as a mounted print in the ESOshop, for anyone who wants this view of the nebula on a wall.

understand.summary: The Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope observed the nebula through U, B, V and R filters plus sulphur and hydrogen-alpha filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The narrow filters isolate the glow of particular gases, and the exposures gather much more light than the eye, so the nebula shows colour and detail no naked-eye view could.

alt: A wide field of the Carina Nebula's stars and dust, with the star Eta Carinae and the Keyhole Nebula towards the lower left.

caption: The elliptical galaxy NGC 3640 and its companion NGC 3641, imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
story: Galaxies of all shapes and sizes fill this picture, from faint blue smudges to NGC 3640, which looks like a fried egg. Beside it sits a smaller galaxy, NGC 3641, giving the egg what looks like a second yolk. NGC 3640 is an unusual elliptical galaxy about 88 million light-years away, captured with the VLT Survey Telescope at ESO's Paranal Observatory.

Galaxies change over their long lives. They can steal gas and stars from each other or merge completely, and the result is often a distorted shape. NGC 3640 is misshapen and wrapped in diffuse light, scars that hint at a violent past.

Astronomers from the Italian National Institute for Astrophysics turned the VST on the globular clusters of both galaxies. These compact balls of stars often hold some of a galaxy's earliest stars and survive mergers, so they act like fossils. The results confirm that NGC 3640 has swallowed other galaxies before.
explore: NGC 3641 shows no clear distortion in its shape or in its globular clusters. That suggests the two galaxies are passing quickly and not close enough for the larger one to pose a threat, at least for now.

understand.summary: This image comes from the VLT Survey Telescope at Paranal. The source doesn't give the filters or say what the colours represent.
understand.eye: The telescope's exposures collect far more light than the eye, which lets faint features such as the diffuse light around NGC 3640 show up.

scaleExtra: NGC 3640 is about 88 million light-years away, according to ESO.
alt: A field of galaxies of many shapes and sizes around the large, fried-egg-shaped galaxy NGC 3640, with the smaller NGC 3641 beside it.

caption: Airglow and the Milky Way over Cerro Paranal, seen from the VISTA site, Chile
story: Colourful airglow fills the sky over Cerro Paranal, and the Milky Way arcs across the mountain in the centre of the frame. At its top the Very Large Telescope can just about be made out. A trail of dim yellow lights on the ground runs towards the mountain.

Airglow is a faint light in the atmosphere, given off as atoms and molecules combine and release radiation. It shows only where the sky is dark enough for artificial light not to drown it out. That is why it appears so clearly here. ESO's Paranal Observatory lies deep in Chile's Atacama Desert, far from towns, and has some of the darkest skies on Earth.
The photograph was taken by Y. Beletsky from the site of VISTA, ESO's Visible and Infrared Survey Telescope for Astronomy. Airglow was also the subject of the ESOcast 78 video.

understand.summary: This is a night landscape photograph by Y. Beletsky, taken from the VISTA site. The source gives no camera or colour details.
understand.eye: Airglow is faint and shows only where the sky is very dark, and the source does not say how the photograph's colours compare with the naked-eye view.

alt: A mountain with a telescope at its summit under a sky tinted with coloured airglow and crossed by the Milky Way, with a trail of yellow lights leading towards it.

caption: Hickson Compact Group 31, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The bright, distorted object at middle left is really two dwarf galaxies in a head-on collision. Above them lies a cigar-shaped galaxy, joined to the pair by a bridge of star clusters, and a long rope of clusters points to a fourth galaxy at lower right. The bright object at the centre is a foreground star. All four galaxies belong to Hickson Compact Group 31.

After billions of years, these dwarfs are finally coming together, and the encounter has set off a burst of star birth. Thousands of new star clusters are forming in the streams of debris and at the collision site. Their hot, massive young stars pour out ultraviolet light that heats nearby gas and makes it glow.
Encounters like this are usually seen billions of light-years away, which means billions of years in the past. This group is only 166 million light-years from us, so Hubble can study it in detail.
explore: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys resolved the youngest, brightest clusters. The brightest each hold at least 100,000 stars and are under 10 million years old. The galaxies are entering the last stages of assembly and should form one large elliptical galaxy in another billion years. Jane Charlton of Pennsylvania State University led the observations as principal investigator.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed the group in visible and near-infrared light through filters at 435, 606 and 814 nm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared light, which the eye cannot see, and Hubble's sharp view resolves individual star clusters.

alt: A cluster of distorted galaxies linked by chains of bright star clusters, with a bright foreground star at the centre.

caption: The Boomerang Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Faint arcs and ghostly filaments run through the smooth, bow-tie-shaped lobes of the Boomerang Nebula, a young planetary nebula 5000 light-years away in Centaurus. Planetary nebulae form when a star in the last stages of its life casts off gas. The light in the image is starlight from the central star, reflected by dust.

In 1995, Sahai and Nyman used the 15-metre Swedish ESO Submillimetre Telescope in Chile to show it is the coldest place in the Universe yet found. At -272C it is just 1 degree above absolute zero, colder even than the -270C background glow left by the Big Bang.

Keith Taylor and Mike Scarrott named it in 1980, after spotting a slight asymmetry through a ground-based telescope in Australia. Hubble's sharper view suggests the Bow tie Nebula might have fit better. Most planetary nebulae have bubble-like lobes, and this one may simply be too young to have formed them.
explore: The bow-tie shape seems to come from a fierce wind of 500 000 kilometres per hour, blowing ultracold gas away from the dying star. The star has lost up to a thousandth of a solar mass each year for 1500 years, 10-100 times more than similar objects. That rapid expansion made the nebula so cold.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys took a single 1000-second exposure through a green-yellow filter at 606 nm. With one filter, the colour in the image isn't a multi-colour composite.
understand.eye: Hubble's sharp view shows detail that ground-based telescopes could not resolve, which is why earlier observers saw only a slightly lopsided shape.

alt: A faint nebula with two smooth lobes forming a bow-tie shape around a central star, laced with thin arcs and filaments.

caption: Supernova 1987A and the Tarantula Nebula in the Large Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the ESO Schmidt Telescope
story: A very bright star stands out in the middle right of this view of the Tarantula Nebula, which lies in the Large Magellanic Cloud. That star is Supernova 1987A. When the image was taken, the supernova was bright enough to see with the unaided eye.

A supernova is the explosion of a star, and for a time it can outshine huge numbers of ordinary stars. The Large Magellanic Cloud is a small galaxy near our own, and the Tarantula Nebula is a large region of glowing gas within it. The scene lies about 170000 light-years away, in the constellation Dorado.

The photograph was taken with the ESO Schmidt Telescope, a type of telescope built to cover a wide area of sky in one shot. That wide view places the supernova within its surroundings in the Large Magellanic Cloud.

understand.summary: This visible-light image was made with the ESO 1-metre Schmidt telescope. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: At the time, the supernova itself could be seen without a telescope, while the photograph gathers far more light than the eye.

alt: The Tarantula Nebula and surrounding stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud, with one very bright star at middle right.

caption: The crescent Moon and earthshine setting over Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: A thin crescent Moon sets over ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile. Beside the bright sliver, the rest of the Moon's disc glows faintly. This dim light is called earthshine.

Earthshine happens when sunlight bounces off the Earth and lights up the part of the Moon that the Sun is not shining on directly. The Moon then reflects some of that light back to us, so we see our own planet's glow second-hand.

That makes earthshine useful to astronomers. By studying it, they can examine light reflected from Earth as if our planet were an exoplanet, a world orbiting another star, and search it for signs of life. The picture was taken on 27 October 2011, and according to the source it also records the planets Mercury and Venus.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph by Babak Tafreshi of the Moon setting over Paranal. The source gives no camera or colour details.
understand.eye: Earthshine is faint but can often be seen by eye, while a camera exposure brings out the dim part of the Moon's disc more clearly.

alt: A thin crescent Moon, with the rest of its disc faintly lit, setting over an observatory.

caption: A crescent Moon over an Auxiliary Telescope of the VLTI at sunset, Paranal Observatory
story: A faint crescent Moon hangs above the round enclosure of one of the four Auxiliary Telescopes at ESO's Paranal Observatory, photographed at sunset by ESO Photo Ambassador Gabriel Brammer.

These four telescopes, together with the four Unit Telescopes of the Very Large Telescope, make up the Very Large Telescope Interferometer, or VLTI. The Unit Telescopes are fixed in place, but each 1.8-metre Auxiliary Telescope can be moved. There are 30 stations on the platform to choose from, allowing a spread of up to 200 metres between them.

That spread is what matters. Interferometry combines the light from several smaller telescopes so that together they act like one much larger instrument, with far sharper resolution. For the VLTI this reaches milliarcsecond resolution, fine enough to make out something two metres across at the distance of the Moon. The round enclosure in the photograph houses one of the telescopes that make this possible.

understand.summary: This is a sunset landscape photograph by Gabriel Brammer. The source gives no camera or colour details.
understand.eye: This photograph records ordinary visible light at sunset, and the source gives no detail on how it was processed.

alt: A round telescope enclosure at sunset with a faint crescent Moon above it.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 3972, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: NGC 3972 is a star-studded spiral galaxy in the constellation Ursa Major, the Great Bear. It lies about 65 million light-years away, so the light reaching us now set out 65 million years ago, around the time the dinosaurs died out.

The galaxy holds two kinds of distance marker. In 2011 astronomers saw a type Ia supernova explode there, though it does not appear in this picture. These explosions all reach the same peak brightness and can be seen across vast distances. NGC 3972 also has many Cepheid variables, pulsating stars whose rhythm of brightening and dimming is closely tied to their true luminosity.

Galaxies with both are especially useful. Comparing the Cepheids with the supernova calibrates how bright type Ia supernovae really are, and that lets astronomers work out distances to far-off galaxies. Accurate distances near and far are needed to pin down how fast the Universe is expanding.
explore: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 took this image in 2015 for a project aimed at improving the precision of the Hubble constant, the number that describes the expansion rate of the Universe.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed NGC 3972 in visible and near-infrared light, through filters from 350 nm to 1.6 μm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared light, which the eye cannot see, and Hubble's exposures gather far more light than an eye can.

scaleExtra: NGC 3972 lies about 65 million light-years from Earth, according to ESA/Hubble.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 1483, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: NGC 1483 has a bright central bulge and hazy arms marked by distinct patches of star formation, while many more distant galaxies scatter the background. Hubble's view shows a barred spiral galaxy, which the source places in the southern constellation Dorado, a name meaning dolphinfish in Spanish.

Dorado hosts the Dorado Group, a loose gathering of an estimated 70 galaxies some 62 million light-years away. It is far bigger than the Local Group, the Milky Way's own group of around 30 galaxies, and comes close to the size of a galaxy cluster. Clusters are the largest structures in the Universe held together by gravity.

Barred spirals take their name from the bar-shaped structure across their centres. They make up about two thirds of all spiral galaxies, the Milky Way included. Recent studies suggest a bar may be a common stage in how spirals form, and possibly a sign that a galaxy has reached full maturity.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed NGC 1483 in blue visible light at 435 nm and near-infrared light at 814 nm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and Hubble's exposures gather far more light than an eye can, revealing many distant background galaxies.

alt: A barred spiral galaxy with a bright centre and faint, patchy arms, with many small distant galaxies behind it.

caption: The Hubble Ultra Deep Field in near-infrared light, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Galaxies scatter across this infrared view, and many of them are very far away and seen as they were long ago. It belongs to the Hubble Ultra Deep Field survey, described at the time as the deepest portrait of the Universe ever made. The view is a narrow core sample reaching across billions of light-years.

The picture comes from Hubble's Near Infrared Camera and Multi-Object Spectrometer. It looks a little farther back in time than the visible-light view of the same field. As space expands, light from remote galaxies is stretched from visible into infrared wavelengths, and some is absorbed by hydrogen between galaxies. The most distant galaxies therefore show up only in infrared.
By comparing infrared and visible images, astronomers hoped to find galaxies from perhaps 400 million years after the Big Bang, when the Universe had reached just 2 to 5 percent of its current age.
explore: From the ground, this patch of Fornax looks largely empty, and it spans just one-tenth the diameter of the full Moon. Only a handful of Milky Way stars appear in it. Looking into it is like peering through a 2.5 metre-long soda straw. Visible-light data from the Advanced Camera for Surveys were added to help tell the galaxies' colours apart.

understand.summary: This composite combines Hubble's near-infrared NICMOS observations at 1.1 and 1.6 μm with visible-light data from the Advanced Camera for Surveys. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, and in ground-based photographs this patch of sky looks largely empty.

alt: A field sprinkled with many small, distant galaxies.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 1448, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: NGC 1448 looks like a glittering oval rather than the round spiral many people picture. It is a spiral galaxy in the little-known constellation Horologium, the Pendulum Clock, about 50 million light-years from Earth, and was photographed by Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3.

The oval shape comes down to viewing angle. The source compares a spiral galaxy to a frisbee spinning slowly in space. When one faces us, we can see a great deal of its detail and structure, as in Hubble's well-known view of Messier 51, the Whirlpool Galaxy.

NGC 1448 is tipped almost edge-on to Earth, so its disc looks squeezed into an oval. The spiral arms still curve out from its dense core, and in Hubble's image they can just about be made out. Seen face-on, NGC 1448 would look far rounder, like the Whirlpool.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed NGC 1448 in visible light through filters at 350, 555 and 814 nm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Hubble's exposures reach far fainter light than an eye at a telescope, bringing out the arms that are hard to see in such a tilted galaxy.

alt: An elongated, nearly edge-on spiral galaxy with a dense core and faint arms curving out from it.

caption: The Wolf-Rayet star WR 124 and its nebula, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A bright star blazes at the centre, marked with the diffraction spikes typical of Webb's Near-infrared Camera. They are caused by the physical structure of the telescope. Around the star spreads a nebula of gas and dust, and background stars and galaxies show through it. The star is Wolf-Rayet 124, or WR 124, a luminous, hot, ageing massive star about 15000 light-years away in Sagitta.

The nebula is made of material the star has thrown off, and its structure records the history of those episodes of mass loss. Instead of smooth shells, it formed from random, lopsided ejections. Bright clumps of gas and dust look like tadpoles swimming towards the star, their tails blown back by its stellar wind.
The two instruments play different roles. NIRCam balances the glare of the star against the fainter material around it, while the Mid-Infrared Instrument, MIRI, brings out the nebula's structure.

understand.summary: This Webb composite combines near-infrared NIRCam and mid-infrared MIRI data. Within each instrument, shorter wavelengths are shown bluer. The 900 nm, 1.5 μm and 7.7 μm filters appear in blue, 2.1, 3.35 and 11 μm in green, and 4.44, 4.7, 12 and 18 μm in red.
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, so these colours are assigned to wavelengths no one could see directly.

alt: A bright star with long spikes of light at the centre of a clumpy cloud of gas and dust, with small tadpole-shaped clumps and background galaxies.

caption: The Danish 1.54-metre telescope reflected in a roadside mirror, La Silla Observatory
story: A domed telescope seems to float in mid-air, as if framed in a roadside picture. The effect is a trick of perspective and clever camerawork. The Danish 1.54-metre telescope is reflected, perfectly framed, in one of the many roadside mirrors around ESO's La Silla Observatory.

In the reflection, the telescope appears to point at the Large Magellanic Cloud, which shows in the upper left. The LMC is a small galaxy close by, in orbit around the Milky Way. A soft green airglow, faint light given off by Earth's atmosphere, sweeps across the sunset sky thanks to the very sensitive technique used. Faint orange halos in the distance mark faraway towns and cities beyond the mountains.
La Silla sits at 2400 metres on the edge of the Chilean Atacama Desert and has been an ESO stronghold since the 1960s. ESO Photo Ambassador Yuri Beletsky took the picture.
explore: La Silla currently runs two four-metre-class telescopes that rank among the most productive in the world, according to ESO. The source describes this reflected view of the Danish telescope as a never-before-seen snapshot of the site.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph by Yuri Beletsky, taken with a very sensitive technique that picks up faint airglow. The source gives no camera or colour details.
understand.eye: The camera records faint light, such as the green airglow and the glow of distant towns, far more strongly than the eye would see it.

alt: A telescope dome reflected in a roadside mirror so it seems to float, under a sunset sky with a faint green glow and the Large Magellanic Cloud at upper left.

caption: The spiral galaxy Messier 95, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: Messier 95 faces us almost head-on, its spiral arms forming a nearly perfect circle around the centre before spreading out like a lion's mane. At the heart of the galaxy glows a bright golden core. The Very Large Telescope captured this galaxy, one of the Leo I group, in the constellation Leo, the Lion.

That core contains a star-forming ring almost 2000 light-years across, where much of the galaxy's star birth takes place. Such rings appear mostly in barred spiral galaxies, a class that includes both Messier 95 and the Milky Way.

Messier 96, the brightest member of the Leo I group, outshines Messier 95 and gives the group its other name, the M 96 group. Around the time this picture was released, Messier 95 became host to a probable supernova, first spotted on 17 March 2012. The observations were made before the explosion, so it is not in the image.
explore: At the time of release, both the galaxy and the supernova sat close to the planet Mars among the stars of Leo, according to ESO. The image was made with the FORS1 instrument through V and I filters.

understand.summary: FORS1 on the Very Large Telescope observed Messier 95 in visible and near-infrared light through V and I filters, with a synthetic green channel. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and the telescope's exposures gather far more light than an eye can.

alt: A face-on spiral galaxy with a golden core and a ring of arms spreading outwards.

caption: The lenticular galaxy NGC 1277 in the Perseus Cluster, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Glowing galaxies fill this frame, with the large lenticular galaxy NGC 1277 at its centre. It is a member of the Perseus Cluster, some 220 million light-years from Earth, which ranks among the most massive objects in the known Universe.

Astronomers have called NGC 1277 a relic of the early Universe, since its stars all seem to have formed about 12 billion years ago. For comparison, the Big Bang is thought to have taken place 13.8 billion years ago. The galaxy holds billions of old, metal-rich stars and many ancient globular clusters, round bundles of stars that circle a galaxy like satellites.

To astronomers, any element heavier than hydrogen and helium counts as a metal. Such elements are forged in massive stars and spread when they explode, so later generations of stars contain more of them. Unusually, most of NGC 1277's globular clusters are red and metal-rich, unlike the blue, metal-poor clusters usually found around galaxies of its size.
explore: Massive galaxies are thought to form in two phases. An early collapse with a burst of star formation makes red, metal-rich clusters, and later gathering of material brings in bluer, metal-poor ones. NGC 1277's red clusters confirm it skipped the second phase, raising questions in a hotly debated field.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed the field in visible light through g, r and z filters at 475, 625 and 850 nm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Hubble's sharp, deep exposures pick out globular clusters around NGC 1277 that an eye at a telescope could not separate from the galaxy's glow.

scaleExtra: The Perseus Cluster lies some 220 million light-years from Earth, according to ESA/Hubble.
alt: A field of glowing galaxies with the large lenticular galaxy NGC 1277 at the centre.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 1637, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: NGC 1637 is a spiral galaxy about 35 million light-years away, pictured here by ESO's Very Large Telescope at Paranal Observatory in Chile. It lies in the constellation Eridanus, the River.

NGC 1637 has its own place in the study of exploding stars. Scientists found a Type II supernova in the galaxy in 1999, and they went on to follow its slow fading over the years that followed. A Type II supernova is the explosion that ends the life of a massive star when its core collapses. Tracking how the light of such an event dims over time helps astronomers understand what happened to the star.
The image was made with the FORS1 instrument on the VLT, which observed the galaxy through blue, visual and red filters, together covering much of the range of light that human eyes can see.

understand.summary: FORS1 on the Very Large Telescope observed NGC 1637 in visible light through B, V and R filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The telescope's exposures gather far more light than an eye could.

alt: The spiral galaxy NGC 1637.

caption: The Swedish–ESO Submillimetre Telescope under the Milky Way, La Silla Observatory
story: The Milky Way stretches across the night sky and seems almost to touch the dish of the Swedish–ESO Submillimetre Telescope, or SEST. The photograph was taken at ESO's La Silla Observatory, 2400 metres up on the outskirts of Chile's Atacama Desert, by A. Ghizzi Panizza.

The band of the Milky Way is shaped by light and darkness. Its bright glow is the light of millions of stars in our galaxy's central region, and the dark patches are clouds of dust that block the light behind them.

SEST was built in 1987 for the Swedish Natural Science Research Council and ESO. This 15-metre radio telescope was, at first light, the only large submillimetre telescope in the southern hemisphere. Over the years it studied everything from comets to stellar nurseries and galaxies. It was decommissioned in 2003, after being overtaken by APEX and ALMA further north in Chile.

understand.summary: This is a night landscape photograph by A. Ghizzi Panizza. The source gives no camera or colour details.
understand.eye: A camera exposure collects far more starlight than the eye, so the Milky Way's bright and dark patches show more strongly than they would to someone standing there.

alt: A large radio dish beneath the band of the Milky Way, which appears to reach down and almost touch it.

caption: The Swedish-ESO Submillimetre Telescope backlit by the Moon, La Silla Observatory
story: The 15-metre dish of the Swedish-ESO Submillimetre Telescope, known as SEST, fills the centre of this photograph, lit from behind by the Moon. Farther away on the right, at the highest point of the mountain, stands the dome of the ESO 3.6-metre telescope.

The antenna dish is so highly polished that it acts like a curved mirror. It holds an upside-down reflection of the sky and of the horizon behind the photographer, so the picture shows two views at once.

The source also names two sky features. The reddish star at the top right is Aldebaran, in the constellation Taurus. The Pleiades star cluster appears just to the right of SEST, at about the two o'clock position. As its name says, SEST was built to observe submillimetre wavelengths, far longer than those the eye can see.

understand.summary: This is a moonlit landscape photograph credited to ESO. The source gives no camera or colour details.
understand.eye: The telescope itself was built for wavelengths the eye cannot see, while this photograph records ordinary visible light.

alt: A large, shiny radio dish backlit by the Moon, reflecting the sky upside down, with a telescope dome on a hilltop to the right and stars above.

caption: Nebulae, the Milky Way and airglow over La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: Pink clouds seem to burst across the sky like fireworks over ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile. They are really nebulae, large gatherings of glowing gas. The bright river of the Milky Way curves from horizon to horizon, with the Magellanic Clouds, two nearby dwarf galaxies, to its right.

On the left, a pale white column of zodiacal light rises from the horizon. It is sunlight scattered by dust in the Solar System. A green glow at the centre is airglow, created by various processes high in Earth's atmosphere.

ESO Photo Ambassador Petr Horálek digitally projected the photograph to fit in as much sky as possible. That is why the roads leading to the 3.58-metre New Technology Telescope on the left and the 3.6-metre telescope on the right look bent. The picture also shows why observatories are built in remote, often harsh places. At La Silla, the sky is so clear and so free of artificial light that all this faint glow comes through.

understand.summary: This is a night landscape photograph by Petr Horálek, digitally projected to show as much of the sky as possible. The source gives no other camera or colour details.
understand.eye: The digital projection bends straight roads and the Milky Way into curves, so the geometry differs from what an eye would see on the spot.

alt: A wide, digitally projected view of the night sky with pink glowing nebulae along the Milky Way, the Magellanic Clouds to its right, a pale column of zodiacal light on the left and green airglow in the centre, above two telescopes and distorted roads.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy NGC 4535, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: NGC 4535 looks almost circular because we see it nearly face-on, set against a background of many faint, distant galaxies. A well-defined bar crosses its centre, and its dust lanes bend sharply before the spiral arms split off from the ends of the bar. The arms are bluish, a sign of many hot young stars, while older, cooler stars give the central bulge a yellower tint.
The galaxy lies in the constellation Virgo and belongs to the Virgo Cluster, a huge gathering of up to 2000 galaxies about 50 million light-years away. It is one of the cluster's largest members.

Smaller amateur telescopes can pick it up, and William Herschel first observed it in 1785. Through such telescopes it looks hazy and ghostly, so the amateur astronomer Leland S. Copeland named it the Lost Galaxy in the 1950s.
explore: The Virgo Cluster is not much wider than the Local Group, the group that includes the Milky Way, but it holds almost fifty times as many galaxies. This visible-light image came from the FORS1 instrument on ESO's 8.2-metre Very Large Telescope.

understand.summary: FORS1 on the 8.2-metre Very Large Telescope observed NGC 4535 in visible light through B and V filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Through a small telescope the galaxy looks hazy and ghostly, while the VLT's exposures bring out its bar, dust lanes and coloured arms.

alt: A nearly circular barred spiral galaxy with bluish arms and a yellowish centre, surrounded by small, faint background galaxies.

caption: The Milky Way rising over Cerro Paranal and the Very Large Telescope, Chile
story: A trail of stars rises across the night sky like smoke from a chimney. It is the Milky Way, our home galaxy, and towards the top it widens and brightens into the star-filled galactic bulge at its heart. The four 8.2-metre Unit Telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope are hard to make out on top of Cerro Paranal in Chile's Atacama Desert.

The site was chosen with great care. It has to be as dry as possible, because water vapour absorbs infrared light and spoils observations. At 2600 metres above sea level, the VLT also has less atmosphere between it and the stars.

Paranal's remote location keeps it largely undisturbed and dark. Even the winding roads that lead across the desert to the observatory are only dimly lit, to avoid unnecessary light pollution. From this viewpoint, the VLT looks more like a very small telescope than a very large one.

understand.summary: This is a night landscape photograph by Babak Tafreshi. The source gives no camera or colour details.
understand.eye: A camera exposure gathers far more starlight than the eye, so the Milky Way appears brighter and more detailed than it would to someone on the mountain.

alt: The Milky Way rising like a column of smoke above Cerro Paranal, where the telescope silhouettes are hard to make out.

caption: The elliptical galaxy NGC 2865, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A faint halo surrounds NGC 2865, an elliptical galaxy just over 100 million light-years away in Hydra, the Sea Serpent. John Herschel discovered it in 1835, and Judy Schmidt entered a version of this image in the Hubble's Hidden Treasures image processing competition.

Elliptical galaxies are usually full of old, dying stars, but NGC 2865 is fairly young and lively. It has a rapidly rotating disc of young stars and metal-rich gas, and an unusually large number of young stars for its type. That suggests a starburst swept through the whole galaxy about one billion years ago.

The starburst was set off by a merger. A spiral galaxy much like the Milky Way combined with an elliptical about three times its mass, the forerunner of NGC 2865. Fresh gas from the spiral revived the ageing elliptical, and it went on to form several new generations of stars. The halo is also a product of that merger. It is cold gas torn from the spiral, now forming an almost closed shell around the galaxy.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed NGC 2865 in visible and near-infrared light at 606 nm and 814 nm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The halo of gas is very faint, and Hubble's exposures reveal far more of it than an eye at a telescope could.

alt: The elliptical galaxy NGC 2865 surrounded by a faint, shell-like halo.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 2906, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Blue speckles dot the swirling arms of the spiral galaxy NGC 2906, mixed with broad swathes of orange. The colours tell astronomers what kinds of stars live there.

The blue specks are massive young stars. They burn through their fuel very quickly and give off hot, blue-tinged light. The orange areas are a mixture of two kinds of star. Some are older stars that have swollen up and cooled down, and others are low-mass stars that were never especially hot in the first place. Because they are cooler, these stars shine with a redder light.

Hubble observed the galaxy while searching for the fading light of supernovae, the explosions of stars, that had occurred recently in nearby galaxies. The source credits Wide Field Camera 3, installed during Hubble's fourth servicing mission in 2009.

understand.summary: The source credits Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, while the image metadata lists the Advanced Camera for Surveys with filters at 606 nm and 814 nm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Hubble's exposures gather far more light than an eye can and separate the colours of individual groups of stars.

alt: A spiral galaxy with blue speckles and orange patches across its arms.
flags: instrument mismatch: caption says WFC3, metadata says ACS

caption: Venus, the crescent Moon and an Auxiliary Telescope at sunrise, Paranal Observatory
story: The rising Sun fills the sky over Cerro Paranal in Chile with orange light. Above the dark outline of the mountains hang a crescent Moon and the bright planet Venus. In front stands the silhouette of an Auxiliary Telescope, part of ESO's Very Large Telescope.
The rest of the Moon's disc can also be seen, faintly lit. This is earthshine, sunlight reflected from the Earth onto the Moon and back to us again.

Babak Tafreshi on the left and Yuri Beletsky on the right, both on the ESO Fulldome Expedition, are setting up their tripods and cameras for the day. Their colleague, ESO Photo Ambassador Petr Horálek, caught the twilight moment. The expedition gathered images for the ESO Supernova Planetarium & Visitor Centre, which at the time was being built at ESO's Headquarters in Garching, near Munich, Germany.

understand.summary: This is a sunrise landscape photograph by Petr Horálek. The source gives no camera or colour details.
understand.eye: This is ordinary visible light, and earthshine can be seen by eye, though a camera can hold the bright crescent and its faint disc in one frame.

alt: Two photographers with tripods and the silhouette of an Auxiliary Telescope under an orange dawn sky, with a crescent Moon and Venus above the mountains.

caption: The galaxy cluster LCDCS 0829, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Strange arcs curve around the galaxy cluster LCDCS-0829. They are images of more distant galaxies, stretched by the cluster's own enormous mass, which acts like a giant magnifying glass. The effect is called gravitational lensing.

Lensing follows from Albert Einstein's general theory of relativity. The mass of the cluster bends the fabric of the Universe, and light from background galaxies travels along that bend. As well as making some objects look bigger and brighter, lensing can create several images of one galaxy and pull them into arcs.

The cluster's odd name comes from the Las Campanas Distant Clusters Survey, carried out in March 1995 with a 1-metre telescope at Las Campanas Observatory in Chile. By scanning a long, narrow strip of the southern sky, it found more than one thousand galaxy clusters, most of them previously unknown.
explore: This deep image combines 36 exposures from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, with a total of 5280 s per filter. The picture spans about 2.8 arcminutes.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys used three filters. Blue light (F475W) is shown in blue, near-infrared light (F814W) in green, and longer-wavelength infrared (F850LP) in red.
understand.eye: Much of this light is infrared and invisible to the eye, and the lensed arcs are far too faint to see without Hubble's long exposures.

alt: A galaxy cluster with thin, curved arcs of light from lensed background galaxies.

caption: The Sculptor Galaxy NGC 253, imaged by the Danish 1.54-metre telescope at La Silla
story: Purple light in this picture of NGC 253 comes from an intense burst of star formation, while a yellowish colour marks dust lit up by young, massive stars. NGC 253, also called the Sculptor Galaxy, is the brightest member of the Sculptor Group. It lies about 13 million light-years from Earth in the constellation Sculptor.

It is known as a starburst galaxy because it is currently forming stars at a high rate. The frenzy of star birth began around 30 million years ago and is still going on, and the purple light traces that activity.

One result is the galaxy's superwind, a stream of energetic material pouring out from its centre into space. The image was made with the 1.5-metre Danish telescope at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile.

understand.summary: This combines visible-light observations through B, V and R filters from the Danish 1.54-metre telescope at La Silla. The source links the purple light to star formation and the yellowish colour to dust lit by young stars, but doesn't give the colour for each filter.
understand.eye: The telescope's exposures collect much more light than the eye, so the faint colours of star-forming regions and dust show far more strongly.

alt: The Sculptor Galaxy, NGC 253, with purple and yellowish areas of light.

caption: The Milky Way over the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory
story: The Milky Way stretches over ESO's Very Large Telescope at Paranal Observatory, in Chile's remote Atacama Desert. The sky is filled with countless stars, dark dust lanes and glowing gas clouds, and below the Milky Way sits the Large Magellanic Cloud, a dwarf galaxy that orbits our own.

At Paranal, the Milky Way can shine brightly enough on a dark night to cast shadows of people and objects on the ground. The rosy red clouds are places where stars are forming. Energetic radiation from newborn stars ionises the hydrogen in the gas and makes it glow.

The VLT, which ESO calls the world's most advanced optical observatory, is made up of four Unit Telescopes, all visible in this photograph, plus four smaller movable Auxiliary Telescopes. One of those appears far off, left of the Unit Telescope in the foreground. Every Unit Telescope has a main mirror 8.2 metres across and can see objects four billion times fainter than the unaided eye can.

understand.summary: This is a night landscape photograph by Petr Horálek. The source gives no camera or colour details.
understand.eye: The eye sees little colour in dim light, so the rosy glow of the gas clouds stands out far more in the photograph, even though the Milky Way at Paranal is bright enough to cast shadows.

alt: The Milky Way, with dark dust lanes and reddish glowing clouds, arching over the Very Large Telescope, with the Large Magellanic Cloud below it.

caption: The emission line galaxy UGC 5797, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The smudge of stars at the centre is UGC 5797, an emission line galaxy, which means it is actively forming stars. As massive, bright blue stars are born, its stellar population is constantly being renewed. Galaxies with lots of star formation often take on a blue tint and keep the cycle of stellar birth going.
Behind UGC 5797 lies a scattering of spiral galaxies. Spirals are rich in dust and gas, the raw material for stars, so they often count as emission line galaxies too.

The background spirals also show how much a galaxy's look depends on the angle we see it from. Their discs can appear very different. Some here face us, revealing the structure of their spiral arms, while the two at bottom left are seen edge-on and look like plain streaks. Many others, in a range of colours and at different tilts, are sprinkled across the frame.
explore: Luca Limatola entered a version of this image in the Hubble's Hidden Treasures image processing competition. The Hubble data come from the Advanced Camera for Surveys, using one visible and one near-infrared filter.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed the field in visible and near-infrared light at 606 nm and 814 nm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and Hubble's exposures gather far more light than an eye can, revealing faint background spirals.

alt: A faint smudge of stars at the centre, surrounded by spiral galaxies at various angles, including two thin edge-on streaks at lower left.

caption: The top of the Horsehead Nebula, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A curving wall of dense, smoky gas and dust runs along the bottom of this close-up, the illuminated top edge of the Horsehead Nebula. Above it, distant stars and galaxies fill the frame, including one large, bright star with six long diffraction spikes, while the background fades from dark red to black. The source calls these the sharpest infrared images of the nebula so far.

Also known as Barnard 33, the Horsehead lies roughly 1300 light-years away in Orion, in the western part of the Orion B molecular cloud. It formed from a collapsing cloud and glows because a nearby hot star lights it up. The surrounding gas has already dispersed, but the pillar is made of denser clumps that erode more slowly. Astronomers estimate that in about five million years it too will fall apart.
It is a well-known photon-dominated region, where ultraviolet light from massive stars heats gas and dust and drives its chemistry.
explore: Because it is nearby and seen almost edge-on, the Horsehead is an ideal place to study how these regions are structured and how their chemistry changes. Astronomers consider it one of the best objects in the sky for studying how radiation interacts with interstellar matter. The image comes from Webb's NIRCam instrument.

understand.summary: This Webb NIRCam image uses eight near-infrared filters from 1.4 to 4.7 μm. Light at 1.4 and 2.5 μm is shown in blue, 3.0 and 3.23 μm in cyan, 3.35 μm in green, 4.3 μm in orange, and 4.05 and 4.7 μm in red.
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, so these colours are assigned to wavelengths no one could see directly.

alt: A curved wall of smoky gas and dust along the bottom, with stars and galaxies above, one bright star with six long spikes, and a background fading from dark red to black.

caption: An ALMA antenna under airglow, the Large Magellanic Cloud and the Milky Way, Chajnantor plateau
story: A single antenna seems to gaze at a many-coloured sky. Green airglow hangs over the horizon, the Large Magellanic Cloud peeks from behind the dish, and the Milky Way sprawls overhead. The antenna is far from alone, though. It belongs to the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, or ALMA, made up of 66 high-precision antennas spread across the Chajnantor plateau high in the Chilean Andes.

The antennas are tuned to millimetre wavelengths, which lie between infrared and radio waves. Human eyes evolved to see visible light, so ALMA's view of the Universe is very different from ours. It picks up light from some of the coldest objects known, including dense star-forming clouds, debris discs around newborn stars and distant galaxies.

ALMA has observed Einstein rings, imaged discs where planets form and found complex organic molecules within such discs. Those findings suggest that our Solar System may not be alone in being able to foster life.

understand.summary: This is a night landscape photograph by Petr Horálek. The source gives no camera or colour details.
understand.eye: The antenna works at millimetre wavelengths that no eye can see, while this photograph records visible light.

alt: A single dish antenna under a night sky with green airglow near the horizon, the Large Magellanic Cloud behind the dish and the Milky Way overhead.

caption: Jupiter, Venus and Mercury aligned over La Silla Observatory at sunset
story: The Sun sets over ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile, leaving a fiery orange glow along the horizon. Just left of centre, three planets line up over the telescopes. According to the source, Jupiter is at the bottom left, almost lost in the sunset, Venus is in the middle and Mercury is at the top right.

David Jones took the picture in June 2013, while observing for five nights with the 3.6-metre New Technology Telescope. He was fortunate to have observing time at just the right moment. The close grouping lasted only a week or so, and he noted that the next such event would come in 2026.

Such alignments come around only once every several years. When three or more celestial objects line up in the sky it is called a syzygy. La Silla sits on the edge of the Atacama Desert in one of the driest places on Earth, where the steady air gives very clear views.
explore: The picture blends two photographs taken with different exposure lengths, which brings out detail across the observatory as the Sun goes down.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph by David Jones, blended from two exposures of different lengths. The source gives no other camera or colour details.
understand.eye: The eye adjusts as it looks around a scene, while this picture blends two exposures of different lengths to show the observing site in detail.

alt: An orange sunset over telescope domes on a mountain, with three points of light in a line just left of centre.

caption: The galaxy cluster RXC J0032.1+1808, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Galaxies glow against the dark like fireflies or floating embers from a bonfire. Together they form RXC J0032.1+1808, a massive cluster of galaxies bound together by gravity, photographed by Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3.

The image comes from RELICS, the Reionization Lensing Cluster Survey, which imaged 41 massive galaxy clusters. Its goal was to find the brightest distant galaxies for the James Webb Space Telescope to follow up.

Webb was built to see in infrared, which matters for the most distant objects. Because the Universe is expanding, light from very distant galaxies is strongly redshifted, stretched towards the red end of the spectrum and beyond, so infrared telescopes are needed to study them. The source compares the galaxies Hubble can reach, billions of years back in time, to toddlers. Webb was designed to reach the babies, the very first galaxies that formed in the Universe.
explore: When this picture was released, the source expected Webb to launch in 2018. The cluster images from RELICS were meant to give the new telescope a ready list of bright, distant galaxies worth studying in detail.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3 observed the cluster in visible and near-infrared light, from 435 nm to 1.6 μm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Much of this light is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and the distant galaxies are far too faint to see without Hubble.

alt: Many glowing galaxies scattered across a dark background.

caption: Stars in the halo of the Andromeda Galaxy, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This field of stars lies in the halo of the Andromeda Galaxy, also known as M31, the nearest spiral galaxy to our own. The halo is a spherical cloud of stars surrounding the galaxy, which is 2.5 million light-years from Earth.

The image was taken with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. At the time it was described as the deepest visible-light image of the sky ever made, and it resolves roughly three hundred thousand individual stars.

Depth matters here because the picture records bright giant stars as well as faint dwarf stars. By looking at how the stars are spread across a range of colours and brightnesses, astronomers can estimate the age of the halo's population. That same method, reading the ages of stars from their colours and brightnesses, is one of the main tools astronomers use to date stellar populations.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed the halo in visible and near-infrared light at 606 nm and 814 nm, with a synthetic green channel. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Individual stars in Andromeda's halo are far too faint to see by eye, and only very deep Hubble exposures can pick them out.

alt: A dense field of countless tiny stars of different colours and brightness.
flags: distance mismatch: metadata says 2 million light-years, caption says 2.5 million

caption: The ESO 1.52-metre telescope peeking out of its dome, La Silla Observatory
story: A telescope peeks out from its dome at La Silla Observatory in Chile. It is the ESO 1.52-metre telescope, which at over 55 years old is one of the oldest telescopes at ESO. It helped lay the foundations for many areas of astronomical research.

Its twin stands at the Observatoire de Haute Provence in France, a telescope of the same 1.52-metre size, and both were designed for stellar spectroscopy, which splits starlight into its colours, and for astrophotography. The La Silla telescope used no fewer than five instruments. One of them, the B&C spectrograph, recorded the spectrum of the comet Hale-Bopp during its passage in 1995, one of the first spectra of a comet on record.
After more than 30 years of service, the telescope was decommissioned in 2002. It still sits in its dome looking out over the vast Atacama Desert.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph of the telescope and its dome by Zdeněk Bardon. The source gives no camera or colour details.
understand.eye: This is a visible-light photograph, and the source gives no detail on how it compares with the view by eye.

alt: A telescope visible through the open slit of its dome, overlooking desert terrain.

caption: The first laser guide star unit launching its beam from the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory
story: A laser beam shoots into the night sky from Unit Telescope 4 of ESO's Very Large Telescope at Paranal. The picture marks first light for the first of four laser guide star units, achieved by the team behind the 4 Laser Guide Star Facility on the night of Wednesday 29 April 2015.

A laser guide star is an artificial point of light created high in the atmosphere. Telescopes can measure how the atmosphere distorts that point and correct for the blurring. This first unit was a key step towards building the full Adaptive Optics Facility, which is designed to sharpen the telescope's view in this way.
The photograph records that milestone at Unit Telescope 4, with the remaining laser units still to follow. Adaptive optics systems cancel the blurring with a mirror that constantly changes shape.

understand.summary: This is a night photograph by J. Girard of the laser in action. The source gives no camera or colour details.
understand.eye: The source gives no exposure details, so it does not say how the beam's brightness in the photograph compares with the view by eye.

alt: A laser beam rising into the night sky from a large telescope enclosure.

caption: The warped spiral galaxy NGC 3190, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: Seen edge-on, the spiral galaxy NGC 3190 has tightly wound arms and a warped form that gives it the look of a gigantic potato crisp. Dark dust lanes cross the galaxy, and between the V they form in its south-western part lies the supernova SN 2002bo.

A second supernova, SN 2002cv, is hidden behind a large amount of dust and cannot be seen, although its position is marked on the image. Both were studied as part of a programme on the physics of Type Ia supernovae, a kind of stellar explosion astronomers use to measure distances.

The picture was taken on 26 March 2003 with the FORS1 instrument on UT2, known as Kueyen, one of the four Unit Telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope. The exposures through B, V, R and I filters add up to 14 minutes. North is at the top and east is to the left.
explore: The picture covers 6.15 x 5 arcminutes. Henri Boffin of ESO extracted the data from the archive, reduced it and carried out the final colour processing of the image.

understand.summary: FORS1 on the Very Large Telescope observed NGC 3190 through B, V, R and I filters, from 440 to 768 nm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The 14 minutes of exposure gather far more light than the eye, though SN 2002cv stays hidden by dust even to the telescope.

alt: An edge-on spiral galaxy with a warped disc and dark dust lanes, with a marked supernova position.

caption: The galaxy NGC 3384, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: NGC 3384 glows softly, rounded and largely featureless, much like a typical elliptical galaxy. Such galaxies seldom show signs of recent star formation and are dominated by old, ageing, reddish stars. That sets them apart from lively spirals like the Milky Way, which hold many young, blue stars in arms that swirl around a bright core.

NGC 3384 has a twist, though. Towards its centre it shows a hint of a disc, in the form of a bar of stars cutting across the middle. Many spiral galaxies have bars too, the Milky Way among them. Bars are thought to channel material through and around the core of a galaxy, helping to keep the activity there going.
The galaxy lies approximately 35 million light-years away in the constellation Leo, the Lion. The picture was taken with the Advanced Camera for Surveys on the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed NGC 3384 through g and z filters at 475 nm and 850 nm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Hubble's exposures gather far more light than an eye can, which helps bring out the hint of a central bar.

alt: A smooth, rounded galaxy with a diffuse glow and a faint bar of stars across its centre.

caption: The galaxy cluster Abell S1077, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Stretched stripes resembling scratches on a lens run through this picture of the galaxy cluster Abell S1077. They are really galaxies behind the cluster, whose light has been heavily distorted by its gravity.

Galaxy clusters are large groups of galaxies, each containing millions of stars, and they are the largest structures in the Universe held together by gravity. So much matter is packed into them that they warp spacetime and bend the path of light passing through. Sometimes this works like a magnifying lens, revealing objects behind the cluster that would otherwise be too faint to detect from Earth.

Astronomers combine Hubble with gravitational lensing to look far back in time to the early Universe. One record holder, the galaxy MACS0647-JD, was seen by Hubble and the Spitzer Space Telescope through a similar lens in the cluster MACS J0647.7+7015. Its light took 13.3 billion years to reach us.
explore: Part of the data behind this image was spotted by Nick Rose in the Hubble's Hidden Treasures image processing competition. The observations come from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3 observed the cluster in near-infrared light, from 814 nm to 1.6 μm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, and the lensed background galaxies are far too faint to see without Hubble.

alt: A galaxy cluster with thin, stretched streaks of light scattered among its galaxies.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 1032 seen edge-on, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Like a wizard's staff set aglow, NGC 1032 cuts across the darkness of space in a narrow, bright stripe. It lies about a hundred million light-years away in the constellation Cetus, the Sea Monster.
The view hides the galaxy's true nature. NGC 1032 is a large spiral, but from Earth its broad disc of gas, dust and stars appears nearly edge-on, so it appears as a narrow stripe.

Several background galaxies are scattered around it. Many are face-on or tilted, showing their spiral arms and bright cores. Those angles reveal a lot about arms and nuclei, but to fully understand a galaxy's three-dimensional structure, astronomers also need an edge-on view like this one. It shows how stars are spread through the galaxy and lets astronomers measure the height of the disc and of the bright, star-filled core.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed NGC 1032 in visible light through filters at 435 nm and 606 nm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Hubble's exposures gather far more light than an eye can, revealing the faint background galaxies around NGC 1032.

alt: A thin, bright edge-on galaxy crossing the frame, with a few small spiral galaxies in the background.

caption: The galaxy cluster Cl 0024+17, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Yellow galaxies crowd the foreground of this picture of the galaxy cluster Cl 0024+17, also catalogued as ZwCl 0024+1652. Around them are faint, distant background galaxies whose light has been bent by the cluster's strong gravity.
