One of these, about twice as far away as the yellow cluster galaxies, has been split into five separate blue arcs.

By mapping how the background light is distorted, astronomers worked out how dark matter is spread through the cluster. That is how an international team using Hubble found a ghostly ring of dark matter, thought to have formed long ago in a huge collision between two massive galaxy clusters.

It was the first time a distribution of dark matter had been found that differs substantially from that of ordinary matter. Dark matter cannot be seen directly, so its presence here is known only from the way its gravity bends light.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed the cluster in visible and near-infrared light through six filters from 435 nm to 850 nm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The dark matter ring itself is invisible in any light, and the lensed background galaxies are far too faint to see without Hubble.

alt: A cluster of yellow galaxies with several thin blue arcs curving around them.

caption: The dwarf irregular galaxy KK 246, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: KK 246 looks like glitter scattered over black velvet, quite unlike a spiral or elliptical galaxy. Also known as ESO 461-036, it is a dwarf irregular galaxy that sits inside the Local Void, a vast stretch of nearly empty space.

KK 246 is the only galaxy known for certain to live in this enormous volume, and 15 more have been tentatively identified there. The many other galaxies visible in the picture lie beyond the void and belong to other groups or clusters.

Cosmic voids are gaps in the web-like structure of the Universe where very few galaxies, or none at all, are found. The Local Void lies next to the Local Group and is at least 150 million light-years across. By comparison, the Milky Way is estimated to be 150 000 light-years across, which gives some idea of how empty this region is.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3 observed the galaxy in visible and near-infrared light, from 606 nm to 1.6 μm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The individual stars of this faint dwarf galaxy are far beyond what the eye can see, and part of the light is infrared.

scaleExtra: The Local Void is at least 150 million light-years across, according to ESA/Hubble.
alt: A loose scattering of faint stars like spilled glitter on a black background, with other small galaxies behind it.

caption: Visitors beside the Auxiliary Telescopes and a Unit Telescope of the Very Large Telescope at sunset, Paranal Observatory
story: A small crowd gathers by the telescopes at ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile to watch the night arrive. For most people sunset ends the working day, but here the real work begins after dark, under a clear sky.

The people look tiny next to the domes on their left. These house the four 1.8-metre Auxiliary Telescopes of the Very Large Telescope array. The biggest structure in the picture is at the far left, a VLT Unit Telescope, which makes the crowd look like ants. The VLT has four of these 8.2-metre telescopes, some of the largest on the planet.

ESO planned to go bigger still with the European Extremely Large Telescope, then expected to see first light in the early 2020s. Its mirror is designed to be 39 metres across, which the source describes as bigger and better eyes on the sky.

understand.summary: This is a sunset landscape photograph by C. Malin. The source gives no camera or colour details.
understand.eye: This photograph records ordinary visible light at sunset, and the source gives no detail on how it was processed.

alt: A small group of people at sunset beside several small telescope domes, with a much larger telescope enclosure at far left.

caption: The starburst galaxy J125013.50+073441.5, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A glittering swirl sits inside a glowing haze that stretches into space in different directions, forming a fuzzy streak. Bright blue regions sparkle along the arms where new stars are being born. The galaxy has the unpoetic name J125013.50+073441.5, and it is a starburst galaxy, one with an unusually high rate of star formation.

Starbursts teach astronomers a lot about how galaxies and stars evolve. They begin with huge amounts of gas that is turned into new stars. The furious pace is only a phase, and once the gas runs out the star birth slows. Hubble has also captured other well-known starbursts, including the Antennae Galaxies and Messier 82, which forms stars ten times faster than the Milky Way.
The data were gathered with Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 for LARS, the Lyman Alpha Reference Sample, which studies how radiation and matter interact in fairly nearby starbursts.
explore: This galaxy is one of the fourteen LARS targets. The study has described how a type of light called Lyman-alpha emission interacts with nearby gas, which affects how that light escapes into space. The results were published by Hayes, Östlin and colleagues in The Astrophysical Journal in 2013.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed the galaxy in ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light at 336, 438 and 775 nm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Ultraviolet light is invisible to the eye, and Hubble's exposures gather far more light than an eye can.

alt: A spiral galaxy with bright blue patches along its arms, wrapped in a hazy glow that stretches into a fuzzy streak.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 5037, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Delicate structures of gas and dust show in fine detail across the spiral galaxy NGC 5037, even though it lies about 150 million light-years from Earth. The galaxy is in the constellation Virgo, and William Herschel first recorded it in 1785.

The detail comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, or WFC3, which gathered the exposures combined into this image. WFC3 is a versatile camera. It can record ultraviolet, visible and infrared light, giving astronomers a wealth of information about whatever it observes.

Astronauts installed WFC3 on Hubble in 2009 during servicing mission 4, the telescope's fifth and final servicing mission. That mission was meant to extend Hubble's life by another five years. When this image was released, 12 years later, both the telescope and the camera were still in active use.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed NGC 5037 in visible light at 606 nm and near-infrared light at 1.6 μm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of this light is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and Hubble's sharp view resolves fine gas and dust structures.

scaleExtra: NGC 5037 lies about 150 million light-years from Earth, according to ESA/Hubble.
alt: The spiral galaxy NGC 5037, with fine structures of gas and dust across its disc.

caption: The southern Milky Way above ALMA antennas, Chajnantor plateau
story: ALMA antennas stand beneath a rich sky on the 5000-metre-high Chajnantor plateau in Chile's Atacama region. According to the source, the view takes in the constellations Carina and Vela, with the Milky Way's dark, wispy dust clouds running from upper left to lower right through the middle of the frame.

The caption points out several stars. The bright orange star at upper left is Suhail in Vela, and the similar orange star at upper middle is Avior in Carina. Nearby, three bright blue stars form an L, the left two in Vela and the right one in Carina. Directly below them, at the centre of the image, glows the pink Carina Nebula.

ESO, the European partner in ALMA, provided 25 of the 66 antennas planned for the finished array. The two nearest the camera, marked DA-43 and DA-41, are European antennas. At the time, the telescope was already observing with part of its array, ahead of completion in 2013.
explore: ESO Photo Ambassador Babak Tafreshi took the picture. He founded The World At Night, a programme that photographs historic sites against the night sky. ALMA brings together Europe, North America and East Asia in partnership with Chile, led by ESO, NRAO and NAOJ, with the Joint ALMA Observatory managing construction and operations.

understand.summary: This is a night landscape photograph by Babak Tafreshi. The source gives no camera or colour details.
understand.eye: A camera exposure brings out colours such as the pink of the Carina Nebula, which the eye sees only faintly, if at all.

alt: Radio antennas under a starry sky with the Milky Way's dark dust lanes running diagonally, orange and blue stars, and a pink glowing nebula at the centre.

caption: The star-forming region NGC 3603 and its central star cluster, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This view shows NGC 3603, a rich region of star formation, and the massive, compact cluster of stars at its centre. The picture was taken with the Advanced Camera for Surveys on the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope.

A box on the image marks the area that astronomers studied in detail to detect how the stars within the cluster are moving. Measuring the motions of stars in a cluster is a way to learn how the cluster holds together and how it may change over time. For that work, the sharpness of Hubble's view is essential, since the stars in such a dense cluster crowd closely together.

According to the image metadata, NGC 3603 lies about 20000 light-years away in the constellation Carina. A star-forming region is a cloud of gas and dust where new stars are being born, and the most massive of them light up the gas around them.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed the region in visible and near-infrared light at 435, 550 and 850 nm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Hubble's sharp view separates many stars in the dense central cluster, and its exposures gather far more light than an eye can.

alt: The star-forming region NGC 3603 with a dense cluster of stars at its centre and a box outlining the studied area.

caption: ALMA antennas under a sky with Alpha Centauri, Antares and Saturn, Chajnantor plateau
story: Two bright stars sit directly above the central antenna in this group of dishes on the Chajnantor plateau in Chile, part of the 66 that make up ALMA, photographed by Y. Beletsky. According to the source, the brighter of the two is Alpha Centauri, a triple star system. At the top of the frame, two bright reddish objects lie just outside the main band of the Milky Way. The left one is Antares, a red giant star in Scorpius. The right one is Saturn, the ringed planet.

One of the most exciting findings of modern astronomy is that the Universe is full of exoplanets, worlds beyond our Solar System. Growing evidence suggests most stars have planets. ESO telescopes and other facilities discovered one, Proxima b, orbiting within the habitable zone of Proxima Centauri, one of Alpha Centauri's three stars. Since no star system lies closer to Earth than Alpha Centauri, Proxima b is the nearest exoplanet ever found.

understand.summary: This is a night landscape photograph by Y. Beletsky. The source gives no camera or colour details.
understand.eye: The planet Proxima b cannot be seen in this photograph or by eye, and the photograph gathers far more light than the eye.

alt: Radio antennas under a starry sky, with two bright stars above the central dish and two reddish points of light near the Milky Way at the top.

caption: Orion, the Pleiades and airglow over La Silla Observatory, Chile
story: This long-exposure photograph takes in the busy site of ESO's La Silla Observatory, the far-off glow of roads and towns in Chile's Atacama Desert, and a faint green airglow, light produced in Earth's upper atmosphere.

Low over the mountains, the source points to the Pleiades open star cluster, known in myth as the Seven Sisters. Directly above them is the constellation Orion, the Hunter. Red patches around the figure of the hunter are huge clouds and arcs of ionised gas, known as emission nebulae, and the Milky Way cuts its way across the sky.

The picture was taken by ESO Photo Ambassador Petr Horálek. It brings together the observatory, the lights of the wider region, the glow of the atmosphere and the stars in one frame. Emission nebulae glow because gas in them is ionised by energetic starlight.

understand.summary: This is a long-exposure night landscape photograph by Petr Horálek. The source gives no other camera or colour details.
understand.eye: The long exposure collects far more light than the eye, so faint features such as the green airglow and red nebulae show far more strongly than they would to an observer.

alt: An observatory on a mountain at night with distant glowing lights, a faint green glow in the sky, a star cluster low over the peaks and a constellation with red patches of gas above it.

caption: The Seyfert galaxy IC 4870, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Bright blue threads ripple through IC 4870 like a misshapen system of lakes. In front of it, nearby stars gleam with diffraction spikes, and a few other galaxies hide among them, looking like stars until you look closely. DeLisle Stewart discovered IC 4870 in 1900, and it lies approximately 28 million light-years away.

The galaxy has an active galactic nucleus, or AGN, a central region so luminous that it can be brighter than all the rest of the galaxy put together. AGNs give off radiation across the whole spectrum, from radio waves to gamma rays, powered by a central supermassive black hole consuming material that strays too close. IC 4870 is a Seyfert galaxy, a kind of AGN with characteristic emission lines.

Hubble has imaged it for several studies of nearby active galaxies. Small-scale structure can reveal traces of collisions and mergers, central bars, nuclear starbursts, jets and outflows, and other links between a nucleus and its surroundings.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed IC 4870 in visible light at 606 nm and 814 nm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Hubble's sharp view resolves small structures near the galaxy's nucleus, and its exposures gather far more light than an eye can.

alt: A galaxy streaked with bright blue threads, surrounded by foreground stars with spikes and a few small background galaxies.

caption: Part of the GOODS-South field, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: More than 45,000 galaxies fill this infrared view of part of GOODS-South, a patch of sky that Hubble and other observatories have studied closely. The Webb image comes from JADES, the JWST Advanced Deep Extragalactic Survey, one of the largest programmes of the telescope's first year of science. It is set to use about 32 days of telescope time hunting for faint, distant galaxies.

Even with data still arriving, JADES has found hundreds of galaxies dating from the Universe's first 600 million years. There are far more of them than observations made before Webb's launch had predicted. That helps astronomers tackle the question of how the first stars and galaxies formed.

The team has also found galaxies from the Epoch of Reionization, when the Universe changed from opaque to transparent. Many show unusually strong emission lines because they are forming great numbers of hot, massive stars.

understand.summary: This Webb NIRCam image uses nine filters. Light at 0.9, 1.15 and 1.5 microns is shown in blue, light at 2.0, 2.77 and 3.35 microns in green, and light at 3.56, 4.1 and 4.44 microns in red.
understand.eye: Most of this light is infrared, invisible to the eye, and the galaxies are far too faint to see without a large telescope.

alt: A field packed with thousands of small, distant galaxies.

caption: The first light of sunrise over the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory
story: Sunrise is just beginning over ESO's Very Large Telescope at Paranal Observatory in Chile. One of the VLT's Unit Telescopes stands at the bottom right, lit by the Moon, and farther off two Auxiliary Telescopes point upwards.

The VLT has four 8.2-metre Unit Telescopes and four movable 1.8-metre Auxiliary Telescopes. Working together they form a giant interferometer, known as the Very Large Telescope Interferometer. A complex system of mirrors in underground tunnels combines their light, revealing details up to 16 times finer than a single Unit Telescope can see.

Astronomer Nicolas Blind took the picture during a visit of a few days in December 2012. He recalls a silence so complete that he could hear only the wind, or perhaps a lost bat, and says the clear sky reminded him how small we are and why he chose astronomy.
explore: Paranal enjoys 330 clear nights a year, and ESO describes the VLT as the world's most productive individual ground-based facility. Blind shared the photograph through the Your ESO Pictures Flickr group, which ESO reviews for its Picture of the Week series.

understand.summary: This is a dawn landscape photograph by Nicolas Blind. The source gives no camera or colour details.
understand.eye: This photograph records ordinary visible light at the start of sunrise, and the source gives no detail on how it was processed.

alt: A large telescope enclosure lit by moonlight at lower right, with two smaller telescopes in the distance under a brightening dawn sky.

caption: The centre of the Milky Way above the ESO 3.6-metre telescope, La Silla Observatory
story: The Milky Way stretches across the frame, a disc-shaped galaxy seen perfectly edge-on. Above the dome of the ESO 3.6-metre telescope, lit by the Moon, rises its yellowish central bulge, partly hidden behind dark clouds of dust. Following the dark lane that climbs from the centre towards the top leads, according to the source, to the reddish nebula around Antares.

Our galaxy holds hundreds of billions of stars along with plenty of gas and dust. The dust absorbs visible light and re-emits it at longer wavelengths, so to our eyes it looks completely opaque. Ancient Andean civilisations saw animal-shaped constellations in these dark lanes. The Galactic Centre lies in Sagittarius and is best seen in the southern winter.
The telescope, inaugurated in 1976, works with the HARPS spectrograph, which ESO calls the world's most precise exoplanet hunter. La Silla was ESO's first site in Chile.
explore: La Silla lies 600 km north of Santiago, at 2400 m on the outskirts of the Atacama Desert, and was the largest observatory of its time. ESO Photo Ambassador Alexandre Santerne took the photograph while the telescope was observing.

understand.summary: This is a night landscape photograph by Alexandre Santerne. The source gives no camera or colour details.
understand.eye: Dust in the Milky Way absorbs visible light and looks opaque to the eye, which is why the lanes appear dark.

alt: A telescope dome lit by moonlight beneath the edge-on band of the Milky Way, with a bright yellowish bulge partly hidden by dark dust lanes.

caption: The field around quasar J0100+2802, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: Thousands of tiny galaxies in varied colours spread across black space, some of the smallest in shades of orange and pink. At the centre sits a small pink object with six diffraction spikes, a little smaller than the blue foreground stars. It is quasar J0100+2802, an active supermassive black hole. The field holds more than 20,000 galaxies and lies between Pisces and Andromeda.

The quasar is so bright that it lights up the gas between it and Webb like a flashlight. The EIGER team studied 117 galaxies from approximately 900 million years after the big bang, concentrating on the 59 in front of the quasar, and the illuminated gas around them.

These galaxies come from shortly before the Era of Reionisation ended. The early Universe's gas cooled over hundreds of millions of years, then became hot, ionised and transparent again. Webb shows galaxies had cleared transparent bubbles around themselves, fully ionising gas within a 2 million light-year radius.
explore: That radius is roughly the distance between the Milky Way and Andromeda. In the following hundred million years the bubbles grew and merged, making the whole Universe transparent. The team plans to study six fields, each centred on a quasar, though these first NIRCam images and spectra are already detailed enough for firm conclusions.

understand.summary: This Webb NIRCam image combines three near-infrared filters. Light at 1.15 μm is shown in blue, 2.0 μm in green and 3.56 μm in red.
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, and nearly all of these galaxies are far too faint and distant to see without Webb.

alt: Thousands of tiny galaxies in orange, pink and other colours on black, with a small pink object with six spikes at the centre and larger blue foreground stars.

caption: The Tarantula Nebula (30 Doradus), imaged by ALMA, the Very Large Telescope and VISTA
story: Bright red-yellow streaks lie across a background of bright stars and light pink clouds of hot gas in this composite of 30 Doradus, the star-forming region also called the Tarantula Nebula.

The background is itself a blend of infrared images from the HAWK-I instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope and from VISTA, the Visible and Infrared Survey Telescope for Astronomy. The infrared view shows the stars and the hot gas around them.

The streaks come from radio observations with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, ALMA. They trace cold, dense gas, the kind of material that could collapse and form new stars. Such gas is the raw material from which stars are made. The nebula's web-like tangle of gas clouds is also what earned it its spidery nickname.

understand.summary: This combines near-infrared images from HAWK-I on the VLT and VISTA with ALMA millimetre observations of carbon monoxide. The ALMA data appear as the red-yellow streaks, and the infrared data form the background of stars and pinkish gas.
understand.eye: Both the infrared and millimetre light are invisible to the eye, so the cold gas mapped by ALMA would not appear in an ordinary view.

alt: A field of bright stars and pale pink gas clouds, overlaid with bright red-yellow streaks of cold gas forming a web-like pattern.

caption: The New Technology Telescope under the Milky Way, La Silla Observatory
story: The New Technology Telescope, or NTT, sits between the arching Milky Way and the dark mountainside of ESO's La Silla Observatory. Since 1989 it has imaged the night sky in fine detail. Recent achievements include observing the merger of two neutron stars, studying the structure of asteroids, analysing hundreds of planetary nebulae and researching planets around other stars.

Bigger mirrors collect more light, but they are harder to keep in perfect shape. Astronomers found that above five metres across, gravity bent mirrors enough to degrade images badly. The NTT, at 3.5 metres, was a pioneer meant to open the way to larger mirrors.

Its key feature is active optics, an idea from ESO engineer Raymond Wilson. A thin, flexible primary mirror sits on supports that push just enough to cancel the distortions caused by gravity. The approach was soon taken up at Keck Observatory in Hawai'i, on its two segmented 10-metre telescopes.
explore: The source calls the NTT's design revolutionary and says it brought huge improvements to ground-based astronomy. Similar technology is still being developed today for some of the largest telescopes in the world.

understand.summary: This is a night landscape photograph by Petr Horálek. The source gives no camera or colour details.
understand.eye: A camera exposure gathers far more starlight than the eye, so the Milky Way appears brighter here than it would to someone on the mountain.

alt: A telescope building on a dark mountainside beneath the arch of the Milky Way.

caption: Part of the Vela supernova remnant, imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
story: Intricate, thread-like structures of glowing gas fill this view of the Vela supernova remnant. They are what remains after a massive star blew itself apart in a powerful explosion around 11 000 years ago.

In a supernova, shock waves ripple out through the surrounding gas and compress it into fine threads. Energy released by the explosion then heats those threads until they shine brightly. The patterns in this picture are the result.

The image is only a small part of a much larger picture made by the VLT Survey Telescope's OmegaCAM instrument, hosted at ESO's Paranal Observatory. The Vela remnant is only 800 light-years from Earth, making it one of the closest examples of such an explosion. Being so near, it can be studied in great detail, helping astronomers learn what happens as massive stars come to the end of their lives.

understand.summary: This image was made with OmegaCAM on the VLT Survey Telescope. The source doesn't give the filters or say what the colours represent.
understand.eye: The telescope's wide-field camera gathers far more light than the eye can.

alt: A tangle of fine, glowing thread-like filaments of gas.

caption: The decommissioned Swedish-ESO Submillimetre Telescope reflecting the night sky, La Silla Observatory
story: The large dish of the Swedish-ESO Submillimetre Telescope, or SEST, still stands at La Silla Observatory in Chile, its reflective surface acting as a mirror for the night sky.

ESO's observatories on the Chilean mountains of La Silla, Paranal and the Chajnantor Plateau host a wide range of telescopes built and run by the organisation's 16 Member States. Over time, older telescopes are overtaken by newer ones, and SEST is one of these veterans.

Built at La Silla in 1987, it broke new ground as the only large telescope in the southern hemisphere studying submillimetre radio waves from objects in the distant Universe. With its 15-metre dish it could study some of the most extreme events and objects in the cosmos. In time, newer facilities on the Chajnantor Plateau, ALMA and APEX, began producing better observations, and SEST was decommissioned in 2003. It no longer observes, but its dish remains on the mountain.

understand.summary: This is a night landscape photograph by Petr Horálek. The source gives no camera or colour details.
understand.eye: A camera exposure picks up the faint night sky and its reflection in the dish more clearly than the eye would in the dark.

alt: A large, shiny radio dish on a mountain at night, reflecting the starry sky.

caption: The Orion Bar region of the Orion Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Two large, bright stars sit at the bottom right of this cloudy scene in the Orion Nebula. Towards the top left, the material is dull, thick and smoky. A brighter purple wall cuts across the bottom right, and beyond it the gas becomes wispier and thinner.

The two stars belong to a cluster called θ² Orionis. The Trapezium Cluster of four hot, massive stars, lies just out of view beyond the top-left corner, and it illuminates the gas seen here. Several proplyds, discs of material around young stars, can be spotted among the clouds.

This view is cut from a larger Hubble mosaic covering the whole Orion Nebula, released in 2006. It has been cropped and aligned to match the same area as observed by the James Webb Space Telescope's NIRCam, so the two telescopes' views can be compared directly.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed the region through five filters. Light at 435 nm is shown in blue, 555 nm in green, hydrogen-alpha and nitrogen light at 658 nm in orange, and 775 and 850 nm in red.
understand.eye: The 658 nm filter isolates the glow of specific gases, and Hubble's sharp view shows fine structure such as the proplyds.

alt: A cloudy nebula with two bright stars at lower right, thick smoky material at upper left and a wall of brighter purple gas crossing the lower right.

caption: The WR 22 and Eta Carinae regions of the Carina Nebula, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope
story: This wide panorama joins two views of the Carina Nebula. On the right is a newer image of the area around the Wolf–Rayet star WR 22. On the left is an earlier picture of the region around Eta Carinae, the star at the heart of the nebula, which the source describes as unique.

A Wolf–Rayet star is a very hot, massive star that is shedding its outer layers in a powerful wind. The nebula around both stars is a vast cloud of gas and dust about 7500 light-years away, in the constellation Carina.

Both images came from the Wide Field Imager, mounted on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile, a camera suited to covering large areas of sky in one shot. The finished panorama is also sold as a mounted print in the ESOshop.

understand.summary: The Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope observed the nebula in visible light through B, V and R filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The camera's exposures gather far more light than the eye can.

alt: A wide panorama of the Carina Nebula, joining the region around WR 22 on the right with the region around Eta Carinae on the left.

caption: The hooked galaxy and its companion in Libra, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: This colour image, titled the hooked galaxy and its companion, shows the galaxy pair catalogued as MCG-01-39-003 and NGC 5917. According to the image metadata, the pair lies about 90 million light-years away in the constellation Libra. A galaxy pair is two galaxies close enough on the sky, and often in space, to be studied together.

The data were gathered with the FORS1 multi-mode instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope for the European Supernova Collaboration in April and May 2006. Observations through four filters, B, V, R and I, were combined to make the colour picture.

The field of view measures 5.6 x 8.3 arcminutes, with north at the top and east to the left. Ferdinando Patat and the Paranal Science team carried out the observations, and Olivia Blanchemain, Henri Boffin and Haennes Heyer of ESO handled the final processing. The European Supernova Collaboration studies supernovae, the explosions that end the lives of some stars.

understand.summary: FORS1 on the Very Large Telescope observed the field through B, V, R and I filters, from 440 to 768 nm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of the light is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and the telescope's exposures gather far more light than an eye can.

alt: The galaxy pair MCG-01-39-003 and NGC 5917, known as the hooked galaxy and its companion.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 3628 in the Leo Triplet, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: NGC 3628 is seen perfectly edge-on, the way we see the Milky Way on a clear night, so its spiral arms are hidden. A dark band of dust runs along its disc and is visibly warped outwards by gravitational tugs from its neighbours. The central bulge is boxy, or peanut-shaped, and appears as a faint X.

The galaxy lies about 35 million light-years away towards Leo and belongs to the Leo Triplet with Messier 65 and Messier 66, which are not in this picture. Charles Messier found those two in 1780, but NGC 3628 is fainter and slipped past his small telescope. William Herschel catalogued it four years later.

The deep image reveals many galaxies of different shapes and colours. A fuzzy blob at the centre is a diffuse satellite galaxy, and fuzzy reddish spots in the halo are globular clusters. Two blue, star-like points near the lower edge are quasars, energetic galaxies billions of light-years away.
explore: Because of its odd shape, NGC 3628 appears as Arp 317 in a 1966 catalogue, the Atlas of Peculiar Galaxies. The image comes from FORS2 on the VLT, combining B, V and R exposures totalling just under an hour. The field is about 7 arcminutes across, too narrow to fit the whole galaxy.

understand.summary: FORS2 on the Very Large Telescope observed NGC 3628 in visible light through B, V and R filters, for a total of just under an hour. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The nearly hour-long exposure collects far more light than the eye, bringing out faint globular clusters, background galaxies and quasars.

alt: An edge-on galaxy with a warped dark dust lane, surrounded by small background galaxies, reddish spots and two blue points near the bottom.

caption: The barred spiral galaxy Messier 77, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: ESO's Very Large Telescope captured Messier 77 face-on. Its glittering arms are crossed by dust lanes, giving a clear look at the structure of this barred spiral galaxy.

The calm appearance hides a more turbulent character, according to the source. The image metadata lists Messier 77 as a Seyfert galaxy, a type of galaxy with an active nucleus, a bright central region powered by material falling towards a supermassive black hole. It lies about 45 million light-years away in the constellation Cetus.

The picture was taken with the FORS2 instrument on the VLT, using visible-light filters along with a hydrogen-alpha filter that picks out the glow of hydrogen gas. In a barred spiral, the arms often begin at the ends of a bar of stars that crosses the centre.

understand.summary: FORS2 on the Very Large Telescope observed Messier 77 through b, v and R filters plus a hydrogen-alpha filter. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The hydrogen-alpha filter isolates the glow of hydrogen gas, and the telescope's exposures gather far more light than an eye can.

alt: A face-on barred spiral galaxy with glittering arms crossed by dust lanes.

caption: The Milky Way over the construction site of the Extremely Large Telescope, Cerro Armazones
story: A clear band of the Milky Way frames the excavated summit of Cerro Armazones almost perfectly. The mountaintop, a construction site when this photograph was taken on 5 July 2019, is the home of ESO's Extremely Large Telescope, or ELT.

Cerro Armazones rises to just over 3000 metres above sea level in Chile's Atacama Desert, only 20 km from ESO's Paranal Observatory and its Very Large Telescope. The peak is isolated, far from the light pollution of cities, and that is what makes the Atacama such a good place for observatories. The clear Milky Way in this picture shows how dark the sky is.

The ELT is ESO's upcoming flagship facility, planned to be the world's biggest eye on the sky. Concrete for its foundation began to be poured in December 2019, and at the time of this picture's release the telescope was expected to be finished later in the decade.

understand.summary: This is a night landscape photograph by Petr Horálek. The source gives no camera or colour details.
understand.eye: A camera exposure gathers far more starlight than the eye, so the Milky Way looks brighter here than it would to someone on the mountain.

alt: The Milky Way arching over a flattened, excavated mountaintop in the desert.

caption: The dwarf irregular galaxy NGC 1156, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: NGC 1156 looks like a cherry tree in blossom. Its many bright blooms are stellar nurseries, where new stars are forming. Energetic light from the newborn stars streams out and strikes nearby pockets of hydrogen gas, which then glows with a characteristic pink colour.

The galaxy lies in the constellation Aries, the Ram. It is classed as a dwarf irregular galaxy, meaning it lacks a clear spiral or rounded shape and is fairly small. Even so, its central region is relatively large and more crowded with stars.

In NGC 1156, some pockets of gas spin the opposite way from the rest of the galaxy. That hints at a close encounter with another galaxy at some point in its past. The other galaxy's gravity, and the turmoil of the encounter, could have scrambled what was probably once a more orderly rotation, leaving the odd motion seen today.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed NGC 1156 in red visible light at 625 nm and through a narrow filter at 658 nm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: The narrow filter isolates the glow of gas in star-forming regions, and Hubble's exposures gather far more light than an eye can.

alt: An irregular galaxy dotted with many bright pink patches like blossoms, with a dense central region.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 2985, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Several tightly wound spiral arms widen as they curl out from the bright core of NGC 2985, fading gradually until they disappear into the emptiness of intergalactic space. The galaxy's nearly perfect symmetry hints at its complex structure.
Galaxies come in many shapes and sizes, and the spiral is one of the key types. NGC 2985 lies roughly 70 million light-years from the Solar System, in the constellation Ursa Major, the Great Bear.

Spirals do not always stay that way. Over very long spans of time, spiral galaxies tend to run into other galaxies, and these encounters often end in mergers. The collisions jumble the winding structures of the original galaxies, smoothing out and rounding their shapes. The resulting galaxies have a beauty of their own, quite different from the spirals they came from.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed NGC 2985 through a narrow filter at 658 nm and a filter at 814 nm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Hubble's exposures gather far more light than an eye can, tracing the faint outer arms as they fade.

alt: A symmetrical spiral galaxy with several tightly wound arms spreading from a bright core and fading outwards.

caption: The galaxy cluster SDSS J1336-0331, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The distortions across this image look like the work of a faulty lens, but they are real. The bright object at the centre is the galaxy cluster SDSS J1336-0331, and its enormous gravity warps the spacetime around it. This strong gravitational lensing bends the light of galaxies behind the cluster into arcs, which helps astronomers study those distant galaxies.

The cluster is interesting in its own right. It was part of a study of star formation in 42 Brightest Cluster Galaxies, or BCGs, the brightest galaxies in their clusters. BCGs usually sit at the centres of their clusters and rank among the Universe's most massive and luminous galaxies. Most are huge ellipticals and are likely to host active galactic nuclei.

The study found evidence that BCGs are fuelled by cold gas. In older BCGs, star formation no longer adds much to their growth, which comes instead through mergers. Violent, gas-rich mergers can trigger intense bursts of star formation.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed the cluster in visible and near-infrared light, from 390 nm to 1.6 μm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Much of this light is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and Hubble's exposures gather far more light than an eye can.

alt: A bright central galaxy cluster surrounded by curved, stretched arcs of light from background galaxies.

caption: The Atacama Pathfinder Experiment under the Milky Way, Chajnantor plateau
story: The Atacama Pathfinder Experiment, or APEX, stands on the Chajnantor plateau, 5000 metres up in the Chilean Andes. Above it, the plane of our galaxy, the Milky Way, stretches across the sky, resembling a band of faint, glowing clouds.
The central region of the Milky Way lies to the left of APEX. According to the source, that is where a supermassive black hole sits at the core of our galaxy.

APEX is run jointly by the Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy, the Onsala Space Observatory and ESO, and ESO is responsible for operating it at Chajnantor. The photograph was taken by Babak Tafreshi for The World At Night. The glow of the Milky Way is the combined light of vast numbers of stars, too distant to pick out one by one.

understand.summary: This is a night landscape photograph by Babak Tafreshi. The source gives no camera or colour details.
understand.eye: A camera exposure gathers far more light than the eye, so the Milky Way's glowing clouds appear brighter than they would to someone on the plateau.

alt: A radio telescope dish under the night sky with the Milky Way stretching across it like a band of faint glowing clouds.

caption: The star cluster NGC 1872 in the Large Magellanic Cloud, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Thousands of stars crowd NGC 1872, a rich star cluster in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy neighbouring our own. This little-studied cluster lies in the constellation Dorado, the Dolphinfish, which is no relation of the dolphin and often appears on menus as mahi-mahi. Scottish astronomer James Dunlop probably spotted it first, in 1826, using a small telescope near Sydney, Australia.

Astronomers value clusters because their stars formed together, at the same time and place, so they share similar ages and starting compositions. Such studies have been vital for understanding how stars evolve, and Hubble extends them beyond the Milky Way to other galaxies of the Local Group.

Star clusters are usually called open or globular, but NGC 1872 shares traits with each type. Its richness matches a typical globular cluster, yet it is much younger, and like many open clusters it has bluer stars. Intermediate clusters like this are common in the Large Magellanic Cloud.
explore: The image came from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, with exposures of 115 s and 90 s. The picture spans about 3.0 by 1.5 arcminutes.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed the cluster through a yellow filter (F555W), shown in blue, and a near-infrared filter (F814W), shown in red.
understand.eye: The near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and the individual stars of a cluster in another galaxy are far too faint to see without Hubble.

alt: A dense, rich cluster of thousands of stars, many of them bluish.

caption: The centre of Stephan's Quintet, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Twisted shapes, dust lanes stretching between galaxies and long strands of stars and gas reaching far beyond the central regions all point to violent encounters. This Hubble close-up shows the central part of Stephan's Quintet, a group of galaxies moulded by tidal interactions, and, according to the source, one of the most exciting star-forming regions in the local Universe.

The quintet is the prototype of the class called compact groups of galaxies, and astronomers have studied it intensively for decades. It is a favourite of amateur astronomers and a challenging target for good hobby telescopes. It even appears, as angelic figures, at the start of the 1946 film It's a Wonderful Life.

At least two of the galaxies have been through high-speed, hit-and-run collisions that ripped stars and gas from their neighbours and flung them into space. New life has come from the wreckage. Over 100 star clusters have emerged from it, along with several dwarf galaxies.
explore: The young clusters each hold up to millions of stars. Hubble's Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 showed them clearly for the first time.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 observed the group in visible and near-infrared light, through filters at 450, 569 and 814 nm. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Through a good hobby telescope the quintet is a challenging, faint target, and Hubble reveals star clusters and filaments no eye could see.

alt: Several distorted galaxies close together, linked by dust lanes and long streams of stars and gas.

caption: The Very Large Telescope at work under the Milky Way, Paranal Observatory
story: The enclosures of the Very Large Telescope's Unit Telescopes turn to work under clear skies at ESO's Paranal Observatory, with the Milky Way overhead. On the left, the smaller Auxiliary Telescopes sit in round white domes, and above them hang the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds.

ESO Photo Ambassador Gabriel Brammer combined several long exposures to capture the faint Milky Way. That also records the enclosures moving as they follow their targets, each shadowed by a ghostly echo. Time passes across the frame too, from a bright evening sky to a dark, star-speckled view towards the left.

Brammer set up his camera in the same spot twice, once at sunset and once later at night, then joined the two panoramas. Each Unit Telescope stands 25 metres tall, and each carries a name from the language of the local Mapuche people. Antu means the Sun, Kueyen the Moon, Melipal the Southern Cross and Yepun Venus.

understand.summary: This panorama by Gabriel Brammer combines several long-exposure shots taken at sunset and later at night. The source gives no other camera or colour details.
understand.eye: No eye could see this at once, because the picture blends different times of evening and records the telescopes' movement as ghostly echoes.

alt: A panorama of large telescope enclosures with ghostly motion echoes under the Milky Way, small white domes at left beneath the Magellanic Clouds, and the sky shading from evening glow to dark night.
